                    ### Question
                    A 23-year-old man presents with fatigue and increased daytime somnolence. He says his symptoms began gradually 6 months ago and have progressively worsened and have begun to interfere with his job as a computer programmer. He is also bothered by episodes of paralysis upon waking from naps and reports visual hallucinations when falling asleep at night. He has been under the care of another physician for the past several months, who prescribed him the standard pharmacotherapy for his most likely diagnosis. However, he has continued to experience an incomplete remission of symptoms and has been advised against increasing the dose of his current medication because of an increased risk of adverse effects. Which of the following side effects is most closely associated with the standard drug treatment for this patient’s most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Cardiac irregularities, nervousness, hallucinations
opb. Loss of concentration, memory impairment
opc. Parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia
opd. Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
ope. Weight gain and metabolic syndrome

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient likely has narcolepsy, characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (episodes of paralysis), and hypnagogic hallucinations. The standard treatments for narcolepsy include stimulants (like modafinil) and sodium oxybate. Modafinil is known to cause side effects such as nervousness and, less commonly, hallucinations. Sodium oxybate can also lead to hallucinations but is primarily used to treat cataplexy and improve nighttime sleep. The side effects most closely associated with standard narcolepsy treatments, particularly stimulants, include nervousness and potential hallucinations. Parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia are not associated with narcolepsy treatments but rather with antipsychotic medications. Therefore, the most relevant side effects from the options provided are nervousness and hallucinations, aligning with the consensus on stimulant use in narcolepsy management.
